extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; literary critics and poets
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging poetry: what counts as 'correct' poetry, the role of imitation, realism of character, the value of vivid imagery and passion, and the rejection of arbitrary formal rules. Aimed at assessing poetic quality across historical schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness (true vs. false)
rubrics_metrics.description: “If by correctness he meant the conforming to rules which have their foundation in truth and in the principles of human nature, then correctness is only another name for excellence. If by correctness be meant the conforming to rules purely arbitrary, correctness may be another name for dulness and absurdity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge 'correctness' by whether rules reflect truth and human nature rather than by arbitrary ceremonial observances. True correctness = fidelity to essential principles; false correctness = slavish adherence to capricious formalities (mala prohibita). Examples of false correctness include narrow legislative rules about metre, couplets, or heroic rhyme that produce dulness rather than excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of imitation / Avoid incorrect imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: “A writer who describes visible objects falsely and violates the propriety of character... may be said, in the high and just sense of the phrase, to write incorrectly. He violates the first great law of his art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure descriptions and character behaviour ring true—avoid grossly implausible images or actions (e.g., making mountains 'nod their drowsy heads' at night, or a dying man delivering an unnatural rant). Models of correct imitation: Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Milton (free from such violations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to character and realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should resemble real human beings; avoid rendering persons as mere names or declamatory types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer portrayals that present characters with believable motives, speech, and behaviour (Troilus and Cressida compared favourably to Racine’s Iphigenie because Shakespeare’s Greeks are 'human beings' while Racine’s are 'mere names'). Evaluate whether dramatis personae feel alive rather than schematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of arbitrary formal constraints (e.g., dramatic unities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules like the dramatic unities of place and time, or rigid prescriptions about line-end punctuation and couplet pauses, are arbitrary canons that often impede the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not privilege compliance with historically contingent formal rules over the work's capacity to develop character, narrative, and emotion. Anti-patterns: insisting on the unities so strictly that complex characters (e.g., Hamlet) could not exist; proscribing redundant syllables, banning similes categorically, or mandating punctuation schemes that harm poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as poetry's end; judge by how well it imitates nature and the human heart
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry is...imitation. It is an art analogous in many respects to the art of painting, sculpture, and acting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry by its success in representing both the external world and the inner life (passions, character, moral situations). Recognize the unique capacity of words to render the deeper and more complex parts of human nature that other arts cannot fully reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotive power and vivid imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetry of the age may be prized for presenting far more vivid images and exciting the passions more strongly than that of a prior age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the poet’s ability to create vivid sensory images and to move the reader emotionally. Consider whether images are original, precise, and effective in stirring feeling rather than merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and creative power (not necessarily opposed to correctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The supposed incompatibility between correctness and creative power often arises from abuse of words; correctness grounded in nature does not preclude genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating novelty and correctness as mutually exclusive. Reward inventive forms and ideas that nevertheless respect the essential laws of imitation and human truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity, passion, and choice of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity and strong passion impart inimitable grace even to homely compositions; poets who seek inspiration in 'noble and affecting subjects' expose fertile images not yet hackneyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poet writes from genuine feeling and chooses subjects that naturally elicit strong images and emotions (e.g., Cowper writing about domestic life; Alfieri's devotion to liberty). Anti-patterns include affectation, insincere ornament, and writing about hackneyed, artificial subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of poetic devices (judge by effect, not rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices like similes, redundant syllables, and other ornaments should be judged by their effect on imitation and feeling, not proscribed by arbitrary rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ban or prescribe devices categorically (e.g., the book quotes critics who forbade redundant syllables or insisted on commas at couplet ends). Instead, measure whether such devices help or hinder truthful, vivid representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must serve ends — practical test of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy: 'The end of fencing is to hit, of medicine to cure, of war to conquer' — similarly, poetic rules are right only insofar as they accomplish poetry’s end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rules and prescriptions by whether they help the poem achieve its aims (imitation, emotion, representation). Discard rules that obstruct the work’s effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical versification and conventional phraseology
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the eighteenth-century tendency to make poetry 'a mere mechanic art'—over-refinement and conventional phrase-making produce feebleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of polished but empty diction, fashionable neatness, and mechanical metres that sacrifice life and passion. Prefer freshness and substance over technical polish divorced from feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical distance and separation of literary from personal character
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is always difficult to separate the literary character of a man who lives in our own time from his personal character... A generation must pass away before it will be possible to form a fair judgment of his books, considered merely as books.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating contemporary authors, allow for the influence of personal scandal and public fashion; recognize that long-term literary reputation may differ from contemporaneous reception. Avoid letting the author's life unduly colour assessment of their works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and ambition — evaluate breadth of imaginative faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: The domain of poetry is 'commensurate with the imaginative faculty' and includes the whole external and internal universe; poetry's range should be considered in assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the work’s imaginative range — its ability to render varied aspects of nature, society, and inner life. Large ambition that succeeds in representing broad human experience is a quality to reward.
